title: Solving quadratics over the complex numbers
log: 2026-11-01T08:04:35Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The bank's discriminant point only says a negative discriminant gives no real roots, while this point must teach finding the complex conjugate roots, which is a new step rather than a small change.

draft.title: Solving quadratics over the complex numbers
card: The discriminant of ax² + bx + c is Δ = b² − 4ac. If Δ is negative, there are no real roots, but there are two complex roots.
Use the quadratic formula: z = (−b ± √Δ) ÷ 2a. Write √(negative number) using i, where i² = −1. For example, √(−16) = 4i.
The two roots are conjugates: they have the same real part and opposite imaginary parts, as in p + qi and p − qi. This holds when a, b and c are all real.
draft.remember: Negative discriminant: two complex roots, found with the formula, and they are conjugates.

a.q: Solve z² + 6z + 10 = 0. What are the roots?
a.why: Δ = 36 − 40 = −4, so √Δ = 2i. Then z = (−6 ± 2i) ÷ 2 = −3 ± i. Using 3 ± i comes from dropping the sign of −b.

b.q: A quadratic with real coefficients has one root 5 − 2i. What is true of its other root?
b.why: Real coefficients and a negative discriminant give conjugate roots, so the other root is 5 + 2i. Negating both parts, as in −5 + 2i, is not the conjugate: only the imaginary part changes sign.
b.clue: Only the sign of the imaginary part changes.

final.title: Solving quadratics over the complex numbers
card: The discriminant of \(ax^{2} + bx + c\) is \(\Delta = b^{2} - 4ac\). If \(\Delta\) is negative, there are no real roots, but there are two complex roots.
Use the quadratic formula: \(z = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}\). Write the square root of a negative number using \(i\), where \(i^{2} = -1\). For example, \(\sqrt{-16} = 4i\).
The two roots are conjugates: they have the same real part and opposite imaginary parts, as in \(p + qi\) and \(p - qi\). This holds when \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are all real.
final.remember: Negative discriminant: two complex roots, found with the formula, and they are conjugates.

a.why: \(\Delta = 36 - 40 = -4\), so \(\sqrt{\Delta} = 2i\). Then \(z = \frac{-6 \pm 2i}{2} = -3 \pm i\). Using \(3 \pm i\) comes from dropping the sign of \(-b\).

b.q: A quadratic with real coefficients has one root \(5 - 2i\). What is true of its other root?
b.why: Real coefficients and a negative discriminant give conjugate roots, so the other root is \(5 + 2i\). Negating both parts, as in \(-5 + 2i\), is not the conjugate: only the imaginary part changes sign.
b.clue: Only the sign of the imaginary part changes.
